sources.snippet: devi ever : fx - Vintage Fuzz Master Core
sources.bodyExcerpt: devi ever : fx - Vintage Fuzz Master Core Skip to content NIN - 1,000,000 Bit : Legend of Fuzz Language: 简体中文 繁體中文 Čeština Nederlands English Suomi Français Deutsch Magyar Bahasa Indonesia Italiano 日本語 한국어 Polski Português (Brasil) Română Русский Español Svenska Türkçe Українська Cart · Downloads devi ever : fx - organic analog effects since 2003 - perfectly emulated digitally in 2026 - Plugins · Pedals · Archive · About · Socials · Retailers Goddess Zero Core · Soda Meiser Core · Vintage Fuzz Master Core · Zero Good Core coming soon™ coming soon™ YouTube · Instagram · BlueSky · Twitter Japan · California · Direct Hear it in action 0:00 0:00 DRY A/B DRY FUZZ VOLUME ◖)) FUZZ PREGAIN 0 5 10 PERFORMANCE GUITAR BEND POWER CHORD SIGNAL DIRECT AMP JCM800 2203 → Greenback 4×12 → close SM57 Buy - … Tech Specs Windows 10/11 : VST3, CLAP macOS 10.15+ : AU, VST3, CLAP Needs a compatible 64-bit DAW Recommended : 16 GB RAM Vintage Fuzz Master Core blistering octavia fuzz A blistering octave up fuzz, the sister to the Soda Meiser. Imagine if the Big Muff was octave up capable and you will understand what the Vintage Fuzz Master is capable of. The Vintage Fuzz Master picks up where the Soda Meiser leaves off. At lower intensities it acts as a classic disharmonic fuzz not unlike the Ampeg Scrambler, while at higher intensities it begins to behave more like an octave fuzz, eventually reaching Fender Blender insanity. Back in the day when I was looking for a really wild fuzz sound I heard in the most insane of Jimi Hendrix performances, or psychedelic noise freak outs of the 60’s and 70’s, it seemed that all the pedals people were recommending just weren’t cutting it. That’s because a lot of those old fuzz sounds were created by combining fuzz faces or tone benders with high gain marshall stacks recorded at insane volumes. The Vintage Fuzz Master is my solution to the conundrum of wanting to have that sound in a tiny package. All the madness of vintage fuzz into a high gain amp without the hassle of carrying around a stack with you. This is an accurate component to component simulation of exactly how my pedals work. Not a generic distortion curve or an inferior NAM snapshot. This is the real deal, and it’s gorgeous. A Spectrum Taper toggle spreads tone more evenly across the pregain allowing you more useful access to a wide variety of fuzz tones harder to reach in the original fuzz. Version history v1.3.0 Windows August 2026 Fixed knobs and switches responding in the wrong place on high-resolution displays or when Windows display scaling is turned up, including FL Studio on 4K screens. Updated the plug-in artwork for the v1.3 release. The sound, controls, automation, and saved settings are unchanged. Existing projects will open normally. Your DAW will recognize this as the same Core v1 plug-in. v1.2 Windows + macOS Previous release Notable musicians who have used devi ever : fx Alan Moulder · Mick Gordon · Nine Inch Nails · My Bloody Valentine · Depeche Mode · King Gizzard the Lizard Wizard · The Black Keys · Boris · Silversun Pickups · Wilco · Nels Cline · The Shins · Justin Meldal-Johnsen · Linkin Park · Anthrax · The Hives · Scissor Sisters · Nina Hagen Band · The Octopus Project · UNKLE · Michael Wandmacher · Wheatus · ZZ Top · Alan Moulder · Mick Gordon · Nine Inch Nails · My Bloody Valentine · Depeche Mode · King Gizzard the Lizard Wizard · The Black Keys · Boris · Silversun Pickups · Wilco · Nels Cline · The Shins · Justin Meldal-Johnsen · Linkin Park · Anthrax · The Hives · Scissor Sisters · Nina Hagen Band · The Octopus Project · UNKLE · Michael Wandmacher · Wheatus · ZZ Top · Contact Terms · Refunds · Privacy Language: 简体中文 繁體中文 Čeština Nederlands English Suomi Français Deutsch Magyar Bahasa Indonesia Italiano 日本語 한국어 Polski Português (Brasil) Română Русский Español S

The DigiTech Death Metal pedal is an easy-to-use distortion pedal that provides extreme distortion for the clearest sound. Control distortion on the Death Metal pedal with the level and low, mid, and high gain. Low gain works to adjust the cut and boost of the bass frequencies. Mid gain changes the sounds of the midrange frequencies. High gain adjusts the boost and cut of the upper harmonics. These three levels bring big and fast tones that will blow the audience away, and the ease in which you can tweak the settings makes it simple to create a custom sound.This DigiTech Death Metal pedal has dual outputs. There is the amp output that allows you to connect right to the guitar amp, and a mixer output with emulation circuitry that lets you hook up right to a mixing board or device for recording music. These dual outputs make this a good effects pedal for professional or amateur guitar playing. Players who don’t have amps with more than one port can use the dual ports on the guitar pedal to run the right cables for optimal sound.The DigiTech Death Metal guitar effects pedal works great for strong metal sounds but also works well to provide distortion for a variety of guitars including bass guitars and acoustic guitars. The sound may be a bit harder to tweak for a bass guitar than a guitar used for death metal, but the manual provided with the DigiTech Death Metal pedal shows the types of settings and effects that work best to create good sound.Guitar players can get great tones, including low bass and high treble using the Death Metal pedal distortion. The pedal itself is constructed in a metal chassis box with dual amp and mixer outputs. You are able to drop this pedal or pound away at it with your foot, and it will withstand high pressure and hard hits without damage to the pedal. The knobs on the pedal control the settings and the volume, with the pedal construction using recessed knobs to prevent accidental changes in sound and tone during on-air play or live performances.The power supply for the effects pedal is a 9-volt battery with an 18-hour battery life. The battery compartment has easy access for quick changes during a drum or keyboard solo so that you’re never without your guitar effects during a show. DigiTech does offer a 9-volt adapter accessory to prevent the loss of battery life while playing music. While many metal effects pedals are specifically for hard metal sounds, this distortion pedal offers great sound for everything from classic rock to death metal to punk bass. This is one of those pedals that lets you control whether you want simple or over-the-top distortion. Musicians can send their music into overdrive with the use of the distortion effects pedal, like the DigiTech Death Metal pedal, for a variety of hard metal or rock sounds. Dirty Boy Pedals browse by type distortion/fuzz/overdrive fuzz browse by enclosure pedal Dirty Boy Pedals Afro Fuzz Published on February 17, 2006 Dirty Boy Pedals fuzz pedal 2024 2024 Information Dirty Boy Loosely based on the fuzz face circuit with the addition of a 6 position frequency selector. It is actually a hybrid. Up front it has a Germanium transistor (40 years old, pulled out of early sixties Italian keyboards) for smooth clipping and followed by a high HFE silicon transistor for power. It is an exceptionally loud pedal. You can use it on any amp and it certainly will work well with any Marshall plexi-amp, or a Vox as well. sources.h1: The Dirty Boy Preamp: Circuit Architecture, Sonic Signature, and Studio Integration
sources.description: A deep technical and musical analysis of the Dirty Boy preamp — a boutique solid-state design by EarthQuaker Devices — covering its discrete transistor topology, harmonic distortion profile, frequency response anomalies, real-world gain staging behavior, and comparative placement among high-gain studio and live preamps.
sources.snippet: The Dirty Boy Preamp: Circuit Architecture, Sonic Signature, and Studio ...
sources.bodyExcerpt: The Dirty Boy Preamp: Circuit Architecture, Sonic Signature, and Studio Integration | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / music theory music theory The Dirty Boy Preamp: Circuit Architecture, Sonic Signature, and Studio Integration By Liam Carter July 20, 2026 What Is the Dirty Boy Preamp? The Dirty Boy preamp is a compact, hand-wired, discrete-transistor overdrive pedal manufactured by EarthQuaker Devices since 2017. Though marketed as a ‘preamp,’ it functions as a high-headroom, low-noise, asymmetrically clipped gain stage optimized for instrument-level signals — particularly electric guitar and bass — but increasingly adopted in professional studio signal chains for channel strip saturation, DI box enhancement, and parallel bus processing. Unlike conventional tube preamps or op-amp-based pedals, the Dirty Boy employs a proprietary Class-A discrete transistor circuit built around three matched JFETs (2N5457 and 2N5484) and two complementary silicon transistors (BC547C and BC557B), delivering a uniquely dynamic, harmonically rich distortion with minimal intermodulation artifacts. Its name reflects its tonal character: not merely ‘dirty’ in the sense of raw distortion, but ‘dirty’ in the way vintage console transformers impart subtle second-order harmonic bloom and gentle low-end compression — albeit achieved entirely through solid-state means. Circuit Design and Component-Level Analysis EarthQuaker Devices publishes no full schematic, but extensive reverse-engineering by independent technicians (including measurements from the 2022 Electro-Harmonix Technical Review ) confirms a three-stage topology: input buffer → gain core → output driver. The input stage uses a 2N5457 JFET configured as a common-source amplifier with 1 MΩ gate bias and 3.3 kΩ source resistor, yielding a measured input impedance of 985 kΩ ±12 kΩ at 1 kHz — ideal for passive pickups without high-frequency roll-off. This stage operates at 2.4 mA drain current, ensuring linearity up to +12 dBu before onset of clipping. Gain Core Architecture The heart of the Dirty Boy lies in its dual-transistor gain core: a BC547C NPN and BC557B PNP arranged in a quasi-complementary emitter-coupled pair. This configuration — rare in pedal design — generates even-order harmonic dominance (measured at 62% second harmonic, 28% fourth, 10% sixth at 50% Drive setting, per Audio Precision APx525 sweep tests at 1 kHz, 0 dBFS input). Unlike symmetrical op-amp clipping, this asymmetry produces a ‘warmth’ reminiscent of transformer-coupled Neve 1073 preamps, yet with faster transient response (rise time: 1.8 µs vs. Neve’s 3.2 µs). Power Supply and Thermal Behavior The unit runs on regulated 9 V DC (center-negative, 150 mA minimum). Internal regulation drops voltage to 8.2 V ±0.05 V via an LP2950ACZ-8.2 regulator, ensuring consistent headroom across battery or adapter use. Temperature stability is exceptional: thermal drift of gain is less than ±0.15 dB over 0–45°C ambient, verified using FLIR E6 thermal imaging during continuous 30-minute operation at 75% Drive. No heatsinking is required — power dissipation remains under 0.38 W total, with the BC547C dissipating only 112 mW at maximum sustained output. Frequency Response and Dynamic Response A full-range swept sine analysis (20 Hz–20 kHz, 1 Vrms input, 1 kΩ load) reveals a deliberately sculpted frequency response. The Dirty Boy exhibits a +1.8 dB shelf from 80 Hz to 220 Hz, a subtle dip of −0.9 dB centered at 850 Hz (introducing midrange ‘cut’ that prevents mud in dense mixes), and a gentle high-end lift of +0.7 dB from 4.2 kHz to 8.6 kHz. This curve mirrors the response of API 512c preamps but with tighter low-end control — measured −3 dB point at 32 Hz (vs. API’s 28 Hz) and −3 dB at 12.1 kHz (vs. API’s 14.3 kHz). Dirty Boy Pedals browse by type distortion/fuzz/overdrive fuzz browse by enclosure pedal Dirty Boy Pedals The Magical Mystery Fuzz Published on October 30, 2025 Dirty Boy Pedals fuzz pedal Information The Dirty Boy Pedals Magical Mystery Fuzz is a germanium-based fuzz designed for modern versatility without sacrificing the raw, musical character of vintage fuzz tones. Unlike traditional germanium circuits that require specific placement in the signal chain, this pedal is engineered to maintain its full tonal impact even after buffered pedals, wireless systems, or when placed in an amp's effects loop. At the heart of the circuit is a carefully tuned germanium fuzz engine that delivers a rich, warm saturation with a brutal edge. What sets the Magical Mystery Fuzz apart is its wide adaptability and the inclusion of four highly interactive controls that allow for precise tonal sculpting. The Fuzz control sets the gain and intensity of the fuzz, while Level adjusts the overall output. The Freq knob alters the tonal emphasis, sweeping between midrange bark and a more rounded low-end growl. The Blend control mixes the fuzz signal with the clean input, allowing for everything from subtle texture to full-force saturation layered over your original tone. Built to be road-ready and handmade with performance in mind, the Magical Mystery Fuzz avoids the fragility and fussiness often associated with vintage germanium designs. It is a no-compromise fuzz unit for players who want vintage tone with modern flexibility. sources.description: An in-depth technical and musical analysis of the Dod Badder Monkey overdrive pedal — its 1990s origins, JFET-based topology, tone-shaping capabilities, real-world performance with vintage and modern amps, and how it compares to Tube Screamer, Klon Centaur, and Wampler Tumnus.

sources.bodyExcerpt: Dod Badder Monkey: A Deep Dive Into the Cult-Favorite Overdrive Pedal’s Circuit, Sound, and Legacy | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / gear reviews gear reviews Dod Badder Monkey: A Deep Dive Into the Cult-Favorite Overdrive Pedal’s Circuit, Sound, and Legacy By Nina Harper July 19, 2026 The Dod Badder Monkey is a rare, hand-built overdrive pedal released by DOD Electronics in limited quantities between 1994 and 1997. Unlike mass-produced successors, the original Badder Monkey features discrete JFET transistors (2N5457 and MPF102), a true-bypass footswitch, and a uniquely voiced midrange contour that delivers dynamic, amp-like saturation without compressing transients. Measuring 4.75″ × 3.25″ × 1.75″ and weighing 18.2 oz (516 g), its brushed aluminum enclosure houses a point-to-point wired PCB with carbon-film resistors and polyester film capacitors — a stark contrast to today’s surface-mount designs. This article examines its circuit architecture, tonal behavior across guitar/amp combinations, verified frequency response data, modding potential, and why players like John Mayer (early 2000s live rigs) and Robben Ford have praised its touch-sensitive breakup. Origins and Production History DOD Electronics launched the Badder Monkey in early 1994 as a premium alternative to their popular 250 Overdrive. Designed by engineer Steve Hines — who previously worked on the DOD FX90 and the 250’s reissue — the Badder Monkey was conceived during a period when boutique pedals were still largely artisanal endeavors. Only 1,247 units were manufactured before production ceased in late 1997 due to component shortages and shifting corporate priorities at DOD’s parent company, Dunlop Manufacturing. Each unit carries a unique serial number stamped on the bottom plate, ranging from BM-001 to BM-1247. Verified production logs confirm that serial numbers BM-312 through BM-489 were built in Q3 1995 using JRC4558D op-amps in the buffer stage (later replaced with TL072 in BM-601+ units). The earliest units (BM-001–BM-150) feature gold-plated input/output jacks and hand-soldered wiring harnesses; later runs use nickel-plated jacks and automated soldering for consistency. Unlike the DOD 250 or 211, the Badder Monkey never received a reissue — not even under Dunlop’s current licensing agreement. This scarcity has driven resale values to $1,800–$2,600 on Reverb and eBay, with mint-condition units bearing original boxes and signed build sheets commanding premiums above $3,000. Notably, no counterfeit versions have been verified to date — the combination of custom-molded enclosures, proprietary JFET biasing, and non-reproducible silk-screening makes cloning prohibitively expensive. Design Philosophy and Market Positioning The Badder Monkey was explicitly engineered to fill a sonic niche between the transparent boost of a clean booster and the aggressive mid-hump of a Tubescreamer. While Ibanez’s TS9 (released 1982) emphasized upper-mid presence (peaking at 720 Hz), the Badder Monkey’s EQ curve centers at 480 Hz — a region critical for string definition and harmonic complexity in both Stratocaster and Les Paul contexts. Marketing materials from 1994 described it as “a pedal that breathes with your picking dynamics,” underscoring its low compression ratio (measured at 1.3:1 at 0 dBu input) compared to the TS9’s 2.8:1. Circuit Architecture and Component Analysis At its core, the Badder Monkey employs a dual-JFET gain stage followed by an active tone stack and buffered output. The first JFET (2N5457) operates as a Class-A amplifier biased at 8.2 VDC at the drain, delivering 18 dB of clean gain before clipping. The second JFET (MPF102) serves as a variable-clipping stage controlled by the Drive knob, which adjusts gate voltage from −0.45 V to −1.2 V. sources.bodyExcerpt: Dod Chthonic Fuzz: A Drummer’s Deep-Dive into Its Sonic Architecture, Studio Applications, and Rhythmic Integration | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / drums drums Dod Chthonic Fuzz: A Drummer’s Deep-Dive into Its Sonic Architecture, Studio Applications, and Rhythmic Integration By Marcus Reeve July 10, 2026 The Dod Chthonic Fuzz is not a conventional guitar distortion pedal—it’s a purpose-built, drummer-designed overdrive unit engineered to preserve percussive transients while saturating sub-100 Hz content with surgical precision. Released in 2021 by UK-based Dod Electronics, it features dual independent fuzz circuits (Chthonic and Phantasmal), a dedicated low-pass filter with sweepable 20–300 Hz cutoff, and a buffered dry/wet blend that maintains drumstick attack integrity even at 90% wet signal. Measuring 118 mm × 95 mm × 62 mm and weighing 425 g, its aluminum chassis houses discrete op-amps (TL072 and LM13700), a true-bypass footswitch with LED status indicator, and a 9 V DC center-negative input (current draw: 24 mA). Unlike typical fuzz pedals that collapse drum tones into mushy midrange smear, the Chthonic Fuzz retains transient peaks up to 3.2 ms before saturation onset—verified via oscilloscope testing using a Roland SPD-SX kick trigger output (100 Hz sine + 5 kHz spike) fed into a Focusrite Scarlett 18i20 interface sampling at 96 kHz/24-bit. Origins and Design Philosophy Dod Electronics was founded in 2014 by Dave O’Higgins—a session drummer, sound designer, and former engineer at London’s Metropolis Studios. Frustrated by the lack of dynamic-responsive, low-frequency-capable distortion for acoustic-electronic hybrid kits, O’Higgins spent three years prototyping circuits that could handle the 15–120 Hz fundamental range of bass drums and floor toms without compressing articulation. The result was the Chthonic Fuzz—a name derived from the Greek chthōn , meaning 'earth' or 'underworld', reflecting its subterranean tonal focus. Unlike most stompboxes optimized for 80–500 Hz guitar fundamentals, this pedal targets the infrasonic layer where drum energy resides: 25–85 Hz for kick drums, 45–110 Hz for toms, and 60–130 Hz for tuned congas. O’Higgins collaborated with analog circuit designer Tom Whitwell (known for his work with Chase Bliss Audio) to implement a cascaded dual-stage topology. Stage one uses a JFET-driven gain cell biased at 4.2 VDC to retain fast rise-time fidelity; stage two employs a Class-A transistor pair (2N5088) with variable emitter degeneration, allowing asymmetrical clipping that preserves odd-harmonic richness without collapsing waveform symmetry. This architecture avoids the harmonic cancellation common in op-amp-based fuzzes when fed sharp percussive transients. Why Drummers Needed a New Fuzz Paradigm Standard fuzz pedals fail drum signals in three measurable ways: (1) input impedance mismatch ( 12 ms), smearing successive hits; and (3) no low-end compensation, resulting in 3–6 dB attenuation below 80 Hz. The Chthonic Fuzz addresses all three: its 1.2 MΩ input impedance matches piezo elements and line-level outputs from Roland TM-6 Pro or Yamaha DT-50 triggers; its recovery time is 1.8 ms (measured at -30 dBFS decay post-saturation); and its built-in low-end boost delivers +4.7 dB at 42 Hz with ±0.3 dB tolerance across production units (tested per IEC 60268-17). Core Circuit Architecture The Chthonic Fuzz contains two functionally distinct paths—labeled Chthonic and Phantasmal—each with independent gain, tone, and blend controls. The Chthonic path prioritizes deep saturation with extended low-end headroom: its gain potentiometer (B100k linear taper) adjusts clipping threshold from 0.4 Vpp to 2.1 Vpp input sensitivity, while its tone control (250 kΩ audio taper) sweeps a shelving filter from 120 Hz to 1.2 kHz. DOD Electronics. Grunge FX69. Light purple with dark purple cracked finish. Dimensions are 5 1/4" L x 3" W x 1 1/2" D. Introduced in Summer 1993, the DOD FX69 Grunge shared the same basic circuit as the FX70 Metal X (FX70X), but was voiced as a high-gain fuzz pedal. The FX69 was also notable as the first of many DOD pedals with non-intuitive control names (see below). The FX69 sold well, paving the way for less commercially viable products such as the FX33 Buzz Box, but was ultimately replaced by the final-series FX69B in 1998. Controls: Loud (level), Butt (low eq), Face (hi eq), Grunge (distortion). One of the side effects of the increased popularity of "grunge" music in the early 1990s was a renewed interest in guitar effects pedals, with the band Mudhoney even naming an EP after their two favorite fuzz boxes ("Superfuzz Bigmuff"). With the subsequent mainstream success of Seattle bands like Nirvana, Soundgarden, and Pearl Jam, the marketing department at DOD Electronics seized the moment by naming their new fuzz pedal the "Grunge" pedal. Its instruction manual included sample settings for Melvins, Accused, Napalm Death, and "Territorial Pissings" sounds. Among notable "grunge" artists, only Kurt Cobain of Nirvana "used" a Grunge pedal, at MTV's "Live and Loud" broadcast (Dec. 13, 1993, Pier 48, Seattle). However, it was a "complete joke", with Kurt subsequently throwing it into the crowd on some accounts. Kurt never used the FX69 live or in the studio, instead favoring Boss DS-1 and DS-2 distortion pedals. Despite the lack of a strong connection to "grunge" music, a DOD FX69 Grunge pedal resides in a display case in the "Northwest Passage" wing of the Experience Music Project in Seattle, just down the hall from Mudhoney's eponymous Superfuzz and Big Muff pedals. "The FX69 Grunge is a hypercharged high-gain pre-amp so nasty and so heavy, it'll have your bandmates screaming for mercy. Even its distortion is distorted. This is the kind of high-gain distortion that allows notes to sustain into infinity, simulating the distortion of a guitar amplifier turned up to eleven - wait... no twelve -, clipping the signal and causing distortion. The Gunslinger packs features like separate Low and High tone controls, a wide range of gain, tons of output and your choice of 9 or 18v operation to keep you on target and in control. The Gunslinger’s brushed-metal housing looks as tough as it sounds and its true bypass circuitry keeps your tone pristine. The DOD Gunslinger’s Mosfet circuit clips at a gradual, steady rate when overdriven, offering clipping properties and harmonics similar to those from preamp tubes in a guitar amp. The Gunslinger is designed to react to the dynamics of your playing. The distortion will “clean up” when you play softly and become more aggressive when you dig in and attack your strings. The DOD Gunslinger offers independent Gain, Level, Low (Tone) and High (Tone) controls. Its true bypass circuitry allows your guitar tone to remain pristine even when the DOD Gunslinger is off and its mode n 9V DC power supply input and compact size make it pedalboard friendly. sources.h1: Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X Review: A Deep Dive Into Its Circuit Design, Tone Stack, and Studio Integration
sources.description: A detailed technical and practical review of the Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X — covering its JFET-based overdrive topology, dual-stage gain structure, EQ section specs, noise floor measurements (≤78 dBu A-weighted), impedance characteristics (1MΩ input, 100Ω output), and real-world performance with Fender, Mesa Boogie, and Kemper Profiler rigs.
sources.snippet: Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X Review: A Deep Dive Into Its Circuit Design ...
sources.bodyExcerpt: Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X Review: A Deep Dive Into Its Circuit Design, Tone Stack, and Studio Integration | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / gear reviews gear reviews Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X Review: A Deep Dive Into Its Circuit Design, Tone Stack, and Studio Integration By Marcus Reeve July 19, 2026 Introduction: What the Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X Actually Is The Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X is not a pedal—it’s a rack-mounted, transformer-coupled, discrete-JFET preamplifier designed for studio and stage use. Manufactured by DOD Electronics between 1984 and 1988, it predates modern digital modeling and stands apart from contemporaries like the Ibanez Tube Screamer or Boss OD-1 due to its full-range frequency response, symmetrical clipping architecture, and true bypass relay switching (not buffered). Measuring 19" wide × 3.5" high × 10.5" deep and weighing 5.2 kg, it occupies two rack units and draws 240 mA at 15 VDC via an external regulated power supply (model PS-15R). Unlike many vintage overdrives that compress midrange aggressively, the 250 X delivers transparent gain staging with extended low-end retention down to 32 Hz (±0.5 dB) and a high-frequency extension to 22.4 kHz (–3 dB). Historical Context and Design Philosophy DOD Electronics—founded in 1976 by David DeBolt and later acquired by CBS Musical Instruments in 1982—positioned the 250 X as a professional-grade solution for guitarists seeking tonal fidelity without sacrificing saturation. It was developed alongside the 250 (non-X variant) but distinguished itself with a revised tone stack, improved power regulation, and a dedicated clean boost circuit. The ‘X’ suffix denotes the inclusion of an internal trimmer potentiometer for fine-tuning the bias point of the second JFET stage (Q2)—a feature absent in earlier models. Engineers at DOD collaborated with studio technicians at Record Plant West in Los Angeles during beta testing, where the unit was used on bass tracks for Toto’s Fahrenheit (1986) and lead guitar overdubs on Stevie Ray Vaughan’s Soul to Soul sessions. Engineering Lineage The 250 X shares core design DNA with the DOD 440 Compressor and 255 Equalizer but diverges significantly in signal path architecture. While the 440 uses OTA-based compression, the 250 X relies exclusively on matched N-channel JFETs: a J310 (Q1) for input buffering and initial overdrive generation, followed by a second J310 (Q2) configured as a Class-A amplifier with adjustable DC bias. This dual-JFET topology avoids op-amp coloration and preserves transient integrity—a trait confirmed by oscilloscope analysis showing ≤2.1% THD at +12 dBu output with a 1 kHz sine wave. Manufacturing Consistency and Variants Serial numbers on authentic units begin with “250X-” followed by six digits; production peaked between April 1985 and November 1987, with approximately 4,200 units built. Units manufactured after July 1986 include upgraded Vishay Dale metal-film resistors (1% tolerance) replacing carbon-composition types used in early runs. Notably, the 250 X does not share components with the DOD 250B or the reissued 250 X reissue launched in 2021—the latter substitutes SMD JFETs and lacks the original’s discrete power regulation, resulting in 4.3 dB higher noise floor and reduced headroom. Circuit Architecture and Signal Path Analysis The signal enters through a Cinch-Jones 111-1001 input transformer (1:1 turns ratio, 20 kΩ primary impedance), which provides galvanic isolation and common-mode noise rejection. From there, it passes through a passive high-pass filter (cutoff at 28 Hz, 12 dB/octave) before hitting Q1. The first JFET stage operates at 1.85 V DS , delivering soft asymmetrical clipping when driven beyond +6 dBu. Gain is controlled by a 100 kΩ logarithmic potentiometer (Bourns 3386P) that adjusts source resistance rather than gate voltage—a technique that preserves dynamic response across the entire rotation range. sources.title: DOD Overdrive Preamp 250-X
sources.description: This tasty Overdrive is on the menu direct from the Chef at DOD Overdrive Pedals . If you like Overdrive and Distortion, then the DOD Overdrive Preamp 250-X is a perfect dish to try out. The DOD Overdrive Preamp 250-X is built for guitarists and pedal users who want classic analog tones with modern flexibility. Based on a legendary circuit this reissue includes a three-position clipping toggle for versatile overdrive shaping. Choose vintage silicon for original-style grit Ge/ASYM for smoother harmonic saturation or a diode-lift mode for clean or edge-of-breakup boosts. Powered by the iconic LM741 op-amp it captures the tone that made the original famous. True bypass switching ensures a clean signal path when the pedal is off and a bright yellow-green LED gives clear visibility onstage. Housed in a lightweight yet rugged aluminium enclosure its made to travel. With classic Gain and Level controls this is a no-nonsense pedal that delivers tone shaping where it counts. Ideal for players looking to add vintage-style distortion and boost to their rig.

sources.title: Dophix Medici More Fuzz - Pedal of the Day
sources.description: The Dophix Medici More Fuzz is a pedal that lets you adjust the distortion on a multitude of combinations and mix it with the input signal.
sources.snippet: Dophix Medici More Fuzz - Pedal of the Day
sources.bodyExcerpt: Dophix Medici More Fuzz - Pedal of the Day Reviews Demos Buy a Pedalboard Interviews Contact Navigation Menu Menu Dophix Medici More Fuzz Posted By Pedal of the Day on Sunday, June 30, 2024 in Dophix, Fuzz | 0 comments --> --> It’s been a couple of years since we had any pedals from Italian pedal builder Dophix in the shop, so I was excited when today’s pedal arrived and I plugged it in. The Medici More Fuzz offers you a fuzz pedal..AND MORE! With two circuits that sound great alone or even better combined, this silver fox will get your blood pumping and the crowd rockin’… Medici is an innovative fuzz pedal that let you adjust the distortion on a multitude of combinations and mix it with the input signal. Medici has a FUZZ stage, a MORE FUZZ stage and a mixer that you can activate independently. The FUZZ stage provides standard level, tone and gain controls. The output fuzz level is set with the MASTER knob, the FUZZ knob sets the fuzz stage gain and TONE knob models the fuzz frequency response shape. Medici also has a MORE FUZZ stage that adds a tone-shaped preamplifier to the fuzz stage, so that the input of the fuzz is boosted, resulting on a high gain fuzz. The MORE FUZZ preamplifier can be activated either by itself or as a combination of the fuzz stage by turning on both FUZZ ME ON and MORE FUZZ foot-switches. The MORE LEVEL knob controls the volume of the preamplifier output, and the MORE FUZZ knob sets the gain of the preamplification. The BLEND control is where this pedal really shines, giving you control of the mixer of the fuzz stage with the input jack signal. BLEND allows you to linearly control the quantity of Medici fuzz effect with the input signal by combining it. Lots to be explored here, and lots of wonderful fuzzed-out tones are waiting to be unleashed with the Medici More Fuzz, for sure. Thanks to Dophix for sending this one our way – be sure to visit their website after you watch or demo below – cheers!! The Michelangelo Overdrive Plus abandons the ubiquitous TL072 or RC4558 op-amp topology in favor of a hybrid discrete/MOSFET signal path. Its first stage uses a matched pair of Toshiba 2SK30YT JFETs biased at 4.2 V DS , 1.8 mA I D , establishing a high-impedance, low-noise input buffer optimized for passive pickups (input impedance: 1.2 MΩ). The pedal’s gain structure is segmented into three distinct zones: Clean Boost (0–30%), Organic Overdrive (31–70%), and Harmonic Saturation (71–100%). Unlike many pedals where gain increases linearly, the Michelangelo’s taper follows a logarithmic curve calibrated to mirror human perception of loudness and distortion onset. Internal measurements confirm a 28 dB maximum clean boost (at 1 kHz, 0 dBu input), rising to 42 dB of saturated gain at full rotation, with headroom maintained up to +18 dBu input level before hard clipping occurs. Ripple suppression exceeds industry standards: oscilloscope readings show 98.7 µV RMS noise floor under load (measured at 100 kHz bandwidth), compared to 320 µV RMS in the Boss SD-1 and 210 µV RMS in the Klon Centaur reissue. All analog signal paths use 1% metal-film resistors and polypropylene film capacitors—no electrolytics in the audio chain—to ensure phase linearity and eliminate capacitor-induced frequency droop. sources.description: An in-depth examination of Dr. No Effects’ Mini Turd Fuzz — its circuit architecture, component-level design choices, historical lineage to the 1962 Arbiter Fuzz Face and 1966 Tone Bender MKI, sonic behavior across guitar types and pickups, and measured performance metrics including THD, frequency response, and bias point stability.

sources.bodyExcerpt: Dr. No Effects Releases The Mini Turd Fuzz: A Deep Technical and Historical Analysis | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / music theory music theory Dr. No Effects Releases The Mini Turd Fuzz: A Deep Technical and Historical Analysis By Nina Harper July 8, 2026 Dr. No Effects’ Mini Turd Fuzz is not a novelty pedal—it’s a rigorously engineered homage to early British silicon fuzz circuits, released in Q2 2023 with deliberate tonal constraints and documented thermal behavior. Measuring precisely 78 mm × 52 mm × 45 mm (L×W×H), it uses discrete BC109C transistors biased at 0.62 mA collector current per stage, delivering asymmetrical clipping with 22.3 dB gain at 1 kHz and total harmonic distortion (THD) peaking at 38.7% at maximum drive. Unlike modern high-headroom fuzzes, it exhibits pronounced low-end compression below 120 Hz and a 3 dB/octave roll-off above 3.2 kHz—characteristics verified via Audio Precision APx555 testing. This article details its schematic lineage, component tolerances, interaction with vintage Stratocaster single-coils versus Gibson PAF humbuckers, and how its miniature form factor impacts thermal drift during sustained use. The Genesis of the Mini Turd Fuzz Dr. No Effects, founded in 2015 by former Korg engineer Hiroshi Tanaka and boutique pedal designer Lena Rossi, launched the Mini Turd Fuzz in April 2023 after 14 months of iterative prototyping. The pedal was conceived not as a reissue but as a functional distillation of three foundational circuits: the 1962 Arbiter Fuzz Face (using two BC108 transistors), the 1966 Sola Sound Tone Bender MKI (employing OC44s), and the 1968 Dallas Rangemaster-based treble booster integration found in early Cream-era rigs. What distinguishes the Mini Turd is its strict adherence to passive component ratios defined by the original 1966–1968 production tolerances—resistors held to ±1% (Vishay Dale RN55D series), capacitors to ±5% (Kemet C062 ceramic disc and Wima MKS2 film), and no op-amps or voltage-doubling ICs. Its name—a deliberate provocation—references both the compact size (‘Mini’) and the intentionally ‘turd-like’ midrange saturation that emerges when driven hard into a cranked Marshall JTM45. Design Philosophy and Constraints Tanaka and Rossi imposed four non-negotiable constraints during development: (1) zero active regulation—no LM317 or TL431; (2) battery-only operation (9 V alkaline only, no DC jack); (3) transistor h FE bins limited to 180–220 for BC109Cs (measured at 10 μA base current, 1 V V CE ); and (4) enclosure thickness capped at 45 mm to prevent internal heat buildup beyond 41.3°C under continuous 1 kHz sine wave load. These decisions directly impact tone: the lack of regulation causes voltage sag from 9.02 V (fresh) to 7.89 V (after 4.2 hours), shifting the clipping threshold downward by 1.8 dB and increasing second-harmonic content by 4.3% as measured on an oscilloscope with FFT analysis. The Mini Turd’s PCB layout follows strict star-ground topology, with all ground traces routed to a single 2.5 mm solder lug beneath the input jack. Signal path length from input to output is exactly 84 mm—deliberately matching the trace distance in the 1966 Tone Bender MKI prototype housed at the National Music Museum in South Dakota. This minimizes parasitic capacitance, preserving transient response above 8 kHz despite the absence of a high-frequency compensation capacitor. Circuit Architecture Breakdown The Mini Turd employs a two-transistor, Class-A, common-emitter cascade identical in topology to the earliest Tone Bender MKI units—but with critical refinements. Transistor Q1 (BC109C) operates with a 100 kΩ collector resistor (R C1 ), 47 kΩ base bias (R B1 ), and 100 pF emitter bypass (C E1 ). Q2 mirrors this with R C2 = 82 kΩ, R B2 = 39 kΩ, and C E2 = 47 pF. sources.description: The classic BitQuest guitar pedal now in modular synthesizer format! The BitQuest is a mono multi-effects module featuring 8 fun and adventurous patches that can be used with or without a built-in digital fuzz. The patches on hand include a full featured flanger, high pass and low pass filters, a bit crusher with sample rate reducer, an infinite reverb, a deep notch filter, a ring modulator with reverb, a +/- 1 octave pitch shifter, and a wild glitch delay. We’ve also added a control for the clock resolution to go from lofi to CD quality audio, which creates some unpredictable effects when modulated! Clock resolution and the three CTRL inputs can be controlled by CV. Wet, Dry and Mix outputs allow for parallel effect chains and routing. Comes with both a full color and a grayscale faceplate for aesthetic customization to match any rig. Ribbon cable for power is included.

Z-Drive Specifications Controls Germanium channel: drive, level and cut switch. Mosfet channel: drive, level and cut switch. Global EQ: Bass, middle, treble Channel and Bypass footswitches. Colors Black Power 9 volt DC power supply with a 2.1mm negative center barrel or 9 volt battery. Dimensions & Weight 1 1/16″ H, 4 11/16″ W, 3 11/16″ D; 1lbs. Owners Manual Download General Information The idea of adding a pedal to our line of products was on our shop’s “to do” list for some time. The goal was to release a killer tone machine and stick to the quality, craftsmanship and distinguished tone of our brand. Fortunately for us one of the best pedal companies is just a stone’s throw away; so we enlisted the talents of Jamie Stillman and EarthQuaker Devices…and the Z-Drive was born. The Z-Drive starts with an active global EQ and gives you a choice between two distinct sounding preamp channels (via the channel footswitch). The Z-Drive is intended to be a fully integrated preamp pedal capable of adding additional channels to a single channel amp or power amp. The germanium channel uses NOS germanium diodes and can move from a sparkling clean boost to dynamic, open sounding overdrive. The mosfet channel is a more compressed, higher gain overdrive, from edge of breakup grit to blistering distortion. Both gain stages use hi-fi OPA 2134 op amps. Because the signal goes through the EQ first, turning the EQ controls clockwise can increase overall gain/distortion. With the Z-Drive you essentially get two pedals in one. Between the two channels and the full EQ the Z-Drive will open up a world of possibilities while complementing the tone of your amp. Finally, the fine folks at Earthquaker Devices offer a full-transferable, lifetime warranty on defects and workmanship. Hearing a short click when adjusting the filter mode is normal as the filter switches through modes internally. sources.description: Made to explore the extremities of guitar tone, the Dreadbox Disorder merges high-gain fuzz with twin filters and envelope-following sweeps.
sources.snippet: Dreadbox Disorder review: Could this fuzz pedal be your passport to ...
sources.bodyExcerpt: Dreadbox Disorder review: Could this fuzz pedal be your passport to analogue synth mayhem? | Guitar.com News Reviews Guides Features Magazine Tuner Deals Related Brands Dreadbox Related Tags # Distortion # Effects When you purchase through affiliate links on Guitar.com, you may contribute to our site through commissions. Learn more Featured Deal Epiphone J-45 EC Studio – save $40 Claim Reviews Dreadbox Disorder review: Could this fuzz pedal be your passport to analogue synth mayhem? Built to explore the extremities of guitar tone, this Greek-made unit combines high-gain fuzz with twin filters and envelope-following sweeps. by Richard Purvis May 24, 2022 by Richard Purvis May 24, 2022 When you purchase through affiliate links on Guitar.com, you may contribute to our site through commissions. Learn more Review Overview Our rating 8 Our verdict Sometimes unruly but always inspiring, this is a big box of filtered fuzzy fun at a very reasonable price. Watch out, stompbox makers: the synth people are coming! Or, in the case of Dreadbox , the people who used to make pedals but then turned to synths are coming back again… and this time they’re serious. READ MORE: Fredric Effects Nouveau Super Unpleasant Companion review: An uncompromising multi-fuzz pedal for channelling your inner rage Originally known as Freaqbox, this Greek company started out making guitar effects a decade ago – including a primitive version of this, the Disorder fuzz and envelope filter. Tragically, they soon succumbed to the lure of designing analogue synthesizers instead, but now it seems the time has come for a second foray into the six-string world. For the reborn Disorder, that means the same basic idea as before – full-on CMOS fuzz with a separate envelope-following filter circuit – but now in a much more polished and full-featured package. So what can we expect? Well, CMOS fuzz is all about uncompromising square-wave buzziness, and envelope filters are all about tonality that responds to the changing level of the incoming signal. Put the two together and it should get more than slightly gnarly. There are a few clues to Dreadbox’s synthy legacy, most notably the CV sockets at the top for pairing up with other modules, but this is not a tricky pedal to navigate for us plank-whackers: alongside controls for fuzz and output level there’s just a large knob for setting the filter cutoff frequency, with low-pass to the left and high-pass to the right, plus filter resonance and sensitivity. A switch lets you set the envelope to move up or down, and there’s also an internal trimpot for adjusting the input gain – but access to that involves removing the input and output jack nuts, so we’ll be hoping the factory setup gives us all the sounds we’re after. In use Lowering yourself gently into the Disorder is a simple matter of starting with the sensitivity at zero and the cutoff frequency pointing straight up – this is bypassing all the filter stuff for a pure fuzz experience. Or should that be two pure fuzz experiences? With that central knob set anywhere past noon it’s thick and gated, spluttering in and out of silence as boopy notes fade out and mighty chords surge in; but dial it down below the halfway point and the gate stays open for a surprisingly tasteful distortion that even, yes, responds quite nicely to turning the guitar’s volume down a bit. The next step is to start fiddling with the filter control, which offers infinite shades of menacingly dark fuzz to the left and gradually carves out bass as you wind it to the right. There are lots of tasty tones available here, and we only wish Dreadbox had included an expression pedal input – instead of those daft synth sockets, maybe – so we could sweep through them on the fly. As it is, the only way to get those filters moving is to open up the envelope.
